bill.title: A bill to direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services, acting through the Administrator of the Health Resources and Services Administration, to establish a grant program to be known as the Mental Health Licensure Portability Program to award grants to eligible entities, and for other purposes.
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

classification.plainSummary: This bill would direct the Department of Health and Human Services to create a grant program called the Mental Health Licensure Portability Program. The program would award grants to eligible entities, though the bill text provided does not specify what those entities would do with the funds or what specific portability barriers the program aims to address.

industries.rationale: The program targets mental health licensure portability, which would directly affect how mental health providers practice across state lines and their regulatory obligations.
Grant recipients could include educational institutions that train mental health professionals or provide licensure-related services.

plain.whatItDoes: No one has written a summary of this bill yet. All we have is its title, and a title is not a description of a law. To find out what it does, you have to open the bill itself.
plain.whoItTouches: We cannot tell from the labels on this bill who it reaches. The subject is too broad to say.
plain.everydayEffect: Nothing has changed yet. The title alone does not say what would change for you, and this tool will not guess. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: From the bill title, and from the subject labels that library staff put on it. There is no official summary of this bill yet.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
